title: Explore the proposed locations of the land of Uz

edom.name: Near Edom
edom.text: The most common view places Uz in or near Edom, in today's southern Jordan, possibly reaching into northwestern Saudi Arabia. Lamentations 4:21 addresses Edom as living in the land of Uz, and Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman, a name tied to Edom. The shading is broad orientation, not a known border.

hauran.name: Hauran
hauran.text: An old tradition places Job in the Hauran of southern Syria, south of Damascus. It draws on Genesis 10:23, which lists Uz as a son of Aram, and on early Christian sites near Nawa connected with Job. The shading is broad orientation, not a known border.

sirhan.name: Wadi Sirhan
sirhan.text: Some place Uz along Wadi Sirhan, a long desert valley running southeast from eastern Jordan into northern Saudi Arabia. It fits a pastoral people “of the East” on the edge of the desert. The shading is approximate.

sheikhsaad.name: Sheikh Sa'd
sheikhsaad.text: A village near Nawa in southern Syria where early Christian and later local traditions honored Job, including a Monastery of Job. Tradition is not proof that Job lived here, and no archaeological find identifies Uz.

bozrah.name: Bozrah
bozrah.text: The prophets name Bozrah as a leading city of Edom (Isaiah 63:1; Amos 1:12). It is usually identified with Buseirah in southern Jordan. It is shown as a landmark for Edom, not as a site in the book of Job.

jerusalem.name: Jerusalem
jerusalem.text: Shown for orientation. Every proposed location for Uz lies east or southeast of ancient Israel, fitting Job's description as a man of the East.

amman.name: Amman
amman.text: Capital of modern Jordan, shown for orientation between the proposed regions.

damascus.name: Damascus
damascus.text: Capital of modern Syria, shown for orientation north of the Hauran.

chapters.title: A man in the land of Uz
chapters.html:
The book of Job opens by naming Job's homeland, but it never places Uz on a map. It calls Job the greatest man among the people of the East, with seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred donkeys.

Those clues point east or southeast of ancient Israel, to grazing land on the edge of the desert. Scholars have proposed several regions, shaded here as broad possibilities.
quote: In the land of Uz there lived a man whose name was Job.
facts: “People of the East” was a general Hebrew term for peoples living east of Israel, often on the desert fringe (Genesis 29:1; Judges 6:3).
Uz was probably a tribal or pastoral territory rather than a walled city, which is one reason no archaeological site has been identified with it.

chapters.title: The case for Edom
chapters.html:
The most common view places Uz in or near Edom, the hill country east of the Arabah valley in today's southern Jordan, perhaps reaching into northwestern Arabia.

Lamentations 4:21 speaks to Edom as the one who lives in the land of Uz. Job's friend Eliphaz came from Teman, a name closely tied to Edom, and the book's desert imagery fits these dry borderlands.
facts: Genesis 36:28 lists a man named Uz among the Horite clans of Seir, the land later ruled by Edom.
Teman appears as a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:11), and the prophets use Teman as another name for Edom (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 9).

chapters.title: The case for the Hauran
chapters.html:
An ancient tradition places Uz farther north, in the fertile Hauran plain of southern Syria. Genesis 10:23 lists Uz as a son of Aram, the ancestor of the Arameans, and Genesis 22:21 names Uz as the firstborn of Abraham's brother Nahor.

Early Christians honored Job at sites near Nawa, including a Monastery of Job at Sheikh Sa'd. These traditions are old, but they are not proof.
facts: The first-century historian Josephus wrote that Uz, son of Aram, founded Trachonitis and Damascus, both on the edges of the Hauran.
A basalt monument at Sheikh Sa'd long called the “Job Stone” turned out to be an Egyptian victory stele of Pharaoh Ramesses II.

chapters.title: Raiders from the desert
chapters.html:
Job lost his herds to raiders: Sabeans, usually connected with Sheba in southern Arabia, and Chaldeans from Mesopotamia. Such raids fit a region exposed to desert peoples.

Some scholars look to Wadi Sirhan, a long desert valley running southeast from eastern Jordan into northern Arabia. Others see Uz as a broad term that may have covered parts of Edom, Moab and northern Arabia over time.
facts: Wadi Sirhan has long served as a caravan corridor between the Azraq oasis in Jordan and Dumat al-Jandal in northern Saudi Arabia.
Elihu, the young speaker in Job 32, was a Buzite. Jeremiah 25:23 names Buz with the Arabian oases of Dedan and Tema.

chapters.title: A story beyond Israel's borders
chapters.html:
Whichever proposal is right, Job is not an Israelite living in Canaan. He is a man of the wider ancient Near East who worships the true God outside the covenant line.

That setting widens the book's message. God's rule and the reality of human suffering are not limited to Israel. Uz may be hard to find on a map, but it was pictured as a real place where one man's faith was tested.
facts: Ezekiel 14:14 names Job with Noah and Daniel as examples of righteousness.
The New Testament points to Job's perseverance as an example for believers (James 5:11).
